opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a reasonable starting point, but I don't think it can be the end point.

In the short term, building on top of strong international foundation models makes a lot of sense. These models have absorbed an enormous amount of world knowledge, language understanding, and common-sense reasoning, and that's genuinely useful for a robot. If you want a robot to understand an instruction like "tidy up the kitchen," you need that semantic layer, and training it from scratch is extremely expensive. So for a startup, borrowing that capability lets you focus your limited resources on the parts that are actually specific to robotics.

But there are a few problems. The first is control and dependency. If your robot's brain sits on a model you don't own, you're exposed to access restrictions, pricing changes, and policy shifts. Given the current geopolitical environment, that's not a hypothetical risk for Chinese companies. It's something you have to plan around.

The second issue is more technical, and I think more fundamental. Language and vision-language models were trained on internet data, which is mostly text and images. A robot brain isn't only about understanding the world. It has to act in it. Physical interaction, force, contact, timing, and the feedback loop between perception and action are mostly missing from internet data. So even the best general model gives you a "high-level brain." You still need a lot of embodied data and your own training to get the "cerebellum," the part that actually moves well and reliably.

So my view is that international models can serve as scaffolding. Use them to get the product off the ground, learn quickly, and validate scenarios. Meanwhile, you should be building your own data pipeline and your own embodied models. Long term, the competitive moat in robotics won't be the language model. Everyone will have access to decent language models, including increasingly strong open-source and domestic ones. The moat will be the real-world interaction data and the ability to close the loop between hardware, data, and model. China actually has real advantages here, because of the manufacturing supply chain and the sheer number of deployment scenarios.

To sum up, borrowing is fine, but you can't rely on borrowing alone. The companies that win will be the ones that use the borrowed capabilities as a bridge while building the pieces that only they can own.

r001.rationale: The response supports using international models as scaffolding while companies build their own embodied data and models, but it does not present fine-tuning international foundation models on vertical-domain data as a route.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd be cautious about treating it as a "route" at all, honestly. It's more like a scaffold you borrow while you build the real thing.

Let me separate two things. First, is it useful to start from an international foundation model? Absolutely. If you're doing embodied AI today, you need a backbone that understands language, understands images, has some common sense about the physical world. Nobody in their right mind trains that from zero when open-weight models exist. Using them lets a team of twenty people get a robot to follow a natural-language instruction in a few months instead of a few years. That's real value, and pretending otherwise is just posturing.

But second, is that a strategy for building a robot brain? I don't think so, for a few reasons.

The foundation models we're talking about were trained on internet text and images. They've never felt a gripper slip. They have almost no sense of force, contact, timing, or what happens when you push something that's heavier than it looks. The part that actually makes a robot work, the low-level control, the action policies, the ability to recover when something goes wrong, that layer isn't in those models. You have to build it yourself, and you have to build it with data you collect yourself, on your own hardware, in your own factories and homes. So the "brain" people care about is mostly the part no foundation model gives you.

Then there's the dependency problem, which is less about geopolitics than people assume, although that's real too. If your core intelligence lives in someone else's model, every time they change the license, change the architecture, or stop releasing weights, your roadmap breaks. And you can't do deep modifications when you don't control the training recipe. For a software startup that's tolerable. For a company that's bolting intelligence to a physical product with a five-year lifecycle, it's a strange place to put your foundation.

And frankly, Chinese companies have the one asset that matters most here, which is data from the physical world. The density of manufacturing, logistics, and consumer hardware in China means you can collect embodied data at a scale almost nowhere else can. If you spend that advantage just fine-tuning someone else's model, you're turning your strongest card into a weak one.

So my view is: use international models aggressively as a starting point, learn everything you can from them, don't be proud about it. But treat them as a temporary floor, not a ceiling. The companies that will matter in five years are the ones that use that head start to collect their own data and train their own action models, and then gradually replace the borrowed parts. The ones that just wrap an API are going to be in trouble, because their product will be indistinguishable from the next team doing the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response accepts international models as useful starting points, but does not present fine-tuning them on vertical-domain data as a plausible route to a robot brain. It mentions fine-tuning someone else’s model as a weak use of Chinese companies’ data advantage and instead advocates training their own action models.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between using an international foundation model to get started and relying on it as the long-term core of a robot. For getting started, it’s a reasonable route. You can use its language understanding and reasoning capabilities to explore tasks and test whether a product is useful without building everything from scratch.

But a robot brain is more than a model that can answer questions. It has to connect perception to action, respond quickly, and deal with the consequences of mistakes in the physical world. A strong general model doesn’t automatically solve those problems. You still need robot-specific data, control systems, and a reliable way to learn from actual deployments.

For Chinese companies, there’s also the question of how much control they have over that foundation: whether they can deploy it locally, adapt it, manage costs, and maintain access. Those considerations matter much more once you’re shipping a product.

So I see international foundation models as a useful starting point. But the lasting advantage will come from the company’s ability to make a robot perform useful tasks reliably—and to improve it through experience. Access to the same model as everyone else isn’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response calls international foundation models a useful starting point and mentions robot-specific data, but it does not say that fine-tuning those models on vertical-domain data is a plausible route.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between using an international foundation model to get started and relying on it as the long-term core of a robot. As a starting point, it can be very useful. You can draw on its language understanding, visual understanding, and general knowledge instead of building everything from scratch.

But those capabilities don’t automatically translate into reliable action. A model may describe how to pick up a cup, yet controlling a robot requires understanding its particular hardware, responding to feedback, and handling failures safely. That takes robotics data, training, and a great deal of testing in the real environment.

For Chinese companies, there’s also the question of whether access, cost, latency, and deployment terms will remain suitable as the product scales. So I see international models as one useful component. The more important question is whether the company can build its own loop: deploy robots, collect useful data, improve the system, and verify that it performs better. That capability matters more than which foundation model you start with.

r001.rationale: The response presents international models as useful starting components and mentions robotics data and training, but it does not clearly say to fine-tune those models on vertical-domain data.
